title: Multi-tenancy and tenant assignment
summary: Partitioning a corpus into isolated groups so access control and leakage tests are meaningful rather than theatrical.
what: A tenant is the unit of isolation: a role is granted some tenants and must never see the rest.
why: Testing access control needs tenants that actually differ and that hold enough documents for a result set to be measurable. One document per tenant proves nothing.
how: Each document is assigned a tenant deterministically from its source, and the assignment is recorded per document so it can be audited.
in_this_project: 47 tenants over 662 documents. SEC filings partition by filing company, which is the natural unit. RFCs partition by working group. CUAD could not: its 510 contracts come from 463 distinct filers, so one tenant per counterparty would hold about 1.1 documents each. Contract type is used instead — bounded, deterministic from the filename, and semantically coherent, so contracts sharing a tenant genuinely resemble each other, which is the property that makes retrieval under access control behave like the real system rather than like random filtering. Tenants below a 500-chunk floor are folded into a semantic sibling, and every document records both its final tenant and the unmerged original.

rows: 29 kept individually, 6 short filers folded by sector

advantages: Semantic tenants keep embedding clusters realistic
limitations: Natural tenant axes are sometimes unusable
Merging is a judgement call that must be documented

pitfalls: Tenants so small that per-tenant indexes are meaningless
Hash-bucketing tenants, which destroys the clustering that makes tests realistic

use: Access control is part of what is being measured
